newsitem.title: USA: Brain chemical may play role in weight gain - study.
newsitem.headline: Brain chemical may play role in weight gain - study.

text.p: In a finding that may contribute to the search for weight-loss drugs, scientists on Thursday said fat mice lacking a hunger-controlling hormone might be only pleasantly plump if they also lack a specific brain chemical.
If the chemical works in people the same way it does in mice, it may some day be possible to develop a drug that would suppress it and help control obesity.

The genetically defective mice lack a hormone called leptin, believed to affect appetite and metabolism. When the mice are further genetically altered so that they lack a brain chemical called neuropeptide Y (NPY), they get only half as fat as those lacking just leptin.
Dr. Richard Palmiter and colleagues at the University of Washington reported their work in Friday's edition of the journal Science.

The research involves mice lacking leptin and does not necessarily apply to other causes of obesity such as eating a high-fat diet. Nor are scientists confident that leptin, identified about two years ago, works the same in people as it does in mice, co-author Jay Erickson said.

In mice, fat cells release the hormone, which acts in the brain to suppress appetite and stimulate metabolism. Mice that lack leptin do not know when they are full so they eat to excess and become grossly overweight.

But no one understood how the hormone worked in the brain. Suspecting that NPY is the trigger, the researchers bred altered mice that lacked both leptin and NPY and compared them to mice that were only leptin-deficient.

The mice lacking both substances got chubby, but only half as fat as those that just lacked leptin. They also had less severe diabetes. But the fact that they still gained weight strongly suggests NPY is not the only brain chemical involved.
"It's not clear how this will relate to human obesity, but it does raise the possibility that neuropeptide Y is involved in some form in human obesity," Erickson said.
